title: Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States
articleTitle: The Evolution of the Funded Research Exclusion: A Comprehensive Analysis of Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States and its Impact on the Section 41 Research Tax Credit
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: Geosyntec Consultants v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), applies to engineering consultancies and contract researchers claiming the federal R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41. The Eleventh Circuit held that capped cost-plus contracts paying monthly for pre-defined tasks regardless of research success are funded research under § 41(d)(4)(H), disqualifying the credit.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

In Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), aff'g No. 9:12-cv-80334-DLB, 2013 WL 5328479 (S.D. Fla. Apr. 17, 2013), the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit issued a landmark ruling defining the boundaries of the "funded research" exclusion under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulations (Treas. Reg.) § 1.41-4A(d). Addressing an issue of first impression within the circuit, the appellate panel established a rigorous textual standard for determining when a service provider, engineering consultancy, or custom manufacturer bears the requisite "financial risk of failure" to claim the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit. The decision remains a cornerstone of federal tax jurisprudence, frequently cited across federal circuits to invalidate R&D tax credit claims where taxpayers conflate general business or budget-overrun risk with the technical risk of research failure, or where contracts mandate compliance with a professional standard of care rather than objective, verifiable technical outcomes.
Factual Background and the Taxpayer's Claim

The taxpayer, Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. ("Geosyntec"), is a specialized consulting and engineering firm engaged in complex projects involving environmental restoration, natural resources assessment, and geological infrastructure design and cleanup. Between 2002 and 2005, Geosyntec entered into hundreds of varied contracts with its clients, both public and private; its stated business model is the development of innovative and sustainable solutions to environmental issues facing those clients. Following an administrative disallowance by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Geosyntec filed a tax refund suit in 2012 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, seeking a federal income tax refund of $1,677,432 under I.R.C. § 41 for Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) incurred during the 2002 through 2005 tax years.

In the interest of efficiency, Geosyntec and the United States designated six representative contracts for the district court's review to govern the legal determination of whether Geosyntec's client work constituted disqualifying "funded research". The parties further stipulated that the terms of these written contracts controlled the funding inquiry as a pure matter of law without the need for expert testimony, and that a judicial finding that a contract was "funded" would entitle the United States to judgment on that agreement, whereas an "unfunded" determination would necessitate further litigation on additional fact-intensive issues related to Geosyntec's right to the research tax credit. The six representative agreements were divided equally into two distinct commercial pricing structures: three fixed-price contracts, under which Geosyntec was paid a fixed total price for its work, and three cost-plus contracts subject to a maximum ("capped contracts"), under which Geosyntec was paid for its labor and expenses, plus a mark-up, subject to an agreed-upon maximum price.
Procedural History and the Contracts on Appeal

On April 17, 2013, ruling on cross-motions for summary judgment, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida entered an order granting each party's motion for summary judgment in part and denying each in part. As to the three fixed-price contracts, the district court agreed with Geosyntec and found that those contracts were not funded under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), so Geosyntec remained eligible for the research tax credit for qualifying research expenses incurred under them. Conversely, the district court held that the three cost-plus capped contracts were "funded" by Geosyntec's clients, rendering Geosyntec statutorily ineligible to claim QREs incurred under those agreements. Because further litigation would have been necessary to determine whether Geosyntec was in fact entitled to the credit on the fixed-price contracts, the parties instead entered into a settlement, and the district court entered an agreed-upon judgment that allowed Geosyntec a federal income tax refund totaling $255,575, plus statutory interest, for the unfunded fixed-price contracts, denied a refund for the funded capped contracts, and preserved Geosyntec's right to appeal the ruling on the capped contracts; the United States did not appeal the partial denial of its own motion.

Geosyntec appealed the ruling as to only two of the three capped contracts: the Cherry Island Contract and the WM Contract (any challenge regarding the third capped contract, with Pneumo Abex Corporation, was deemed abandoned). Executed with the Delaware Solid Waste Authority (DSWA), the 2001 Cherry Island Contract obligated Geosyntec to design a method for expanding the capacity of the Cherry Island Landfill in Wilmington, Delaware, within its existing footprint; the landfill sat on a soft foundation that limited vertical expansion, and Geosyntec ultimately designed a berm wall and drainage system that allowed the vertical expansion DSWA sought. DSWA agreed to pay Geosyntec "on a cost reimbursement basis" in an amount not to exceed $9,991,578, with each subtask separately priced and capped, and Geosyntec submitted one "approvable invoice" per month for services rendered, verified by project managers for both parties, with DSWA obligated to pay only those sums invoiced for work it approved for payment. The second agreement on appeal, the WM Contract, consisted of a 1997 master services agreement with Waste Management, Inc. (WM) and a 2003 project addendum under which Geosyntec was hired to evaluate a system for remediating contaminated groundwater beneath a warehouse site in Niagara, New York, previously used to manufacture and store weapons and radioactive material. Specifically, the WM Contract obligated Geosyntec to perform laboratory bench tests evaluating the feasibility and performance of enhanced in situ bioremediation (EISB) for groundwater cleanup, and to prepare a report describing its methodology, tabulating test results, interpreting collected data, and discussing site conditions and potential pilot-test designs. The addendum capped the contract price at $18,781, and the WM Contract required payment "upon proper performance of each task" at fixed unit prices as set forth in Geosyntec's estimated budget; Geosyntec submitted monthly progress invoices, WM had forty-five days to pay undisputed amounts, and WM could change the work by written change directive, in which case any necessary increase to the capped price required an addendum executed by the parties.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The federal R&D tax credit, originally enacted under the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (initially codified at 26 U.S.C. § 44F, redesignated as § 30 in 1984, and renumbered as § 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986), provides a tax credit equal to 20% of the excess of a taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year over a statutory base amount. The overarching legislative purpose of I.R.C. § 41 is to incentivize American industry to invest in research by reducing the cost of additional research. However, as with all tax credits, taxpayers who claim the research credit bear the burden of establishing their entitlement to it.

To qualify for the credit, research activities must satisfy the four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)—comprising the I.R.C. § 174 deductible research expenditure test, the technological-in-nature test, the business component improvement test, and the process of experimentation test—and must not fall within the statutory exclusions enumerated in I.R.C. § 41(d)(4). Chief among these exclusions is I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), which disqualifies any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9) directs that the determination of whether research is "funded" is governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3), research performed for a client or third party is considered funded unless two conjunctive regulatory prongs are satisfied. First, under the Financial Risk (Contingency) Prong, amounts payable under the agreement must be "contingent on the success of the research". If payment is contingent on technical success, the regulations treat the client's payment as consideration for a "product or result rather than the performance of the research," allowing the researcher—rather than the client—to treat the incurred costs as QREs, which mirrors the client's contract research disallowance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2). Second, under the Substantial Rights Prong, the taxpayer performing the research must retain "substantial rights in the research". If the researcher confers exclusive rights to the client or retains no right to use the research results without paying the client, the research is funded regardless of risk allocation. In evaluating the Financial Risk Prong, the parties relied heavily on, and the Eleventh Circuit applied, the doctrinal framework established by the Federal Circuit in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), which holds that the Treasury Regulations deliberately allocate the R&D tax credit to the contracting party that bears the financial risk of failure of the research to produce the desired product or result.
The Eleventh Circuit's Final Holding

Reviewing the district court's grant of summary judgment and contractual interpretation de novo, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the judgment in favor of the United States. Writing for a unanimous panel, Circuit Judge Wilson held that under the plain language of both the Cherry Island Contract and the WM Contract, Geosyntec was entitled to monthly payment for pre-defined tasks at pre-defined rates regardless of whether its research ultimately succeeded. Because neither contract conditioned DSWA's or WM's payment obligations on the achievement of successful research outcomes or final technical acceptance of a validated product or result, Geosyntec did not bear the financial risk of its own research failure. Consequently, the capped contracts constituted "funded" research under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), disqualifying Geosyntec from claiming the R&D tax credit.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Geosyntec's capped contracts stemmed from fundamental legal, contractual, and structural deficiencies in how the taxpayer framed its commercial risk and documented its performance obligations. A granular examination of the Eleventh Circuit's opinion reveals five interrelated doctrinal failures that continue to govern IRS examinations and federal tax litigation across the United States.
Conflation of "Cost-of-Performance Risk" with "Financial Risk of Research Failure"

One of Geosyntec's arguments on appeal rested on an economic analysis of its ceiling-price contracts. Geosyntec contended that because its total compensation under the Cherry Island and WM contracts was subject to strict maximum price caps and its billing was tied to incurred costs or fixed unit task prices, it bore substantial financial risk—specifically, the risk that its expenses would exceed the ceiling price, and the loss of any opportunity to make a profit on the research should it come in under budget.

The Eleventh Circuit rejected this argument as misplaced, holding that cost-of-performance is not the financial risk with which § 41 is concerned. Citing Fairchild, the court explained that general business risk, budget overrun exposure, or the potential loss of profit opportunity is legally irrelevant to the funded research inquiry; rather, "the only issue is whether payment was contingent on the success of the research"—that is, the financial risk of failure. The court further noted that the capped contracts' not-to-exceed ceiling prices were not immovable: the Cherry Island Contract allowed claims for additional compensation for necessary out-of-scope work, extra compensation where state environmental authorities imposed "unreasonable demands," and hourly-rate changes for two project phases, while under the WM Contract any change in the work would be accompanied by an agreed price increase and/or time extension.

The second-order implication of this holding is profound: a contract's commercial label—whether "capped," "guaranteed maximum price," or even "fixed-price"—does not automatically confer R&D tax credit eligibility. As the Fifth Circuit subsequently reinforced in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), and the Eighth Circuit confirmed in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024)—both relying heavily on Geosyntec—the "inherently risky" economic nature of a capped or fixed-price contract does not make the underlying research unfunded if the payment mechanism itself is not expressly conditioned on technical research success.
The Fatal Dichotomy Between "Proper Performance" and "Successful Performance"

To overcome the absence of express contingency clauses, Geosyntec argued that its right to payment was implicitly conditioned on success because the contracts required compliance with environmental laws, industry quality standards, and professional standards of care. In the WM Contract, for instance, payment was due "upon proper performance of each task". Geosyntec asserted that, because its clients could dispute sums on its invoices, it had "no legal right" to payment unless it could demonstrate that its work was satisfactory.

The Eleventh Circuit rejected this argument, observing that neither contract equates "proper performance" with "successful performance". In the court's analysis, both contracts required Geosyntec to perform in accordance with the standard of care applicable to like professionals and to deliver work free from negligence, error, and defects. By contrast, the court faulted the Cherry Island Contract for providing "no barometer" by which Geosyntec's performance could be considered successful and no mechanism for evaluation and acceptance or rejection of the delivered design; later decisions such as Meyer, Borgman & Johnson have built on this to describe "successful performance" as meeting detailed, objective technical barometers of success on which payment depends.

The court held that the general standard of care and Geosyntec's assurances that its performance would be free from negligence "do not mandate success". In the WM Contract, Geosyntec was hired to conduct laboratory bench tests to evaluate whether EISB could remediate contaminated groundwater beneath the Niagara warehouse. If Geosyntec executed the laboratory bench tests competently and free from scientific negligence ("proper performance"), WM remained contractually obligated to pay Geosyntec for the labor and material used in conducting the treatability test and preparing the report even if the tests established that EISB was not a feasible process for accelerating groundwater cleanup ("unsuccessful research"). Similarly, under the Cherry Island Contract, the landfill expansion design "was left almost entirely to Geosyntec's professional expertise, informed by Geosyntec's own research and subject to general (and, at times, passive) requirements". Unlike the Fairchild contract, the project did not require installation and integration of specific elements, each task was not subject to complex contract specifications, and Geosyntec's work was not subject to inspection and testing before acceptance; while DSWA had the right to review and comment on certain design work, there was no method for its rejection, so DSWA bore the financial risk of whether the research yielded a viable expansion.
Failure to Meet the Fairchild Standard of Technical Specificity and Acceptance Testing

Throughout its opinion, the Eleventh Circuit measured Geosyntec's contracts against the benchmark established in Fairchild Industries. In Fairchild, the U.S. Air Force contracted with Fairchild to design and produce the T-46A aircraft, with the full-scale development (FSD) phase subdivided into eleven separately-priced contract line items. The Eleventh Circuit highlighted three decisive contractual features present in Fairchild that were wholly absent in Geosyntec. First, the Fairchild agreement contained over 1,000 pages of technical specifications requiring Fairchild to meet specific design, construction, quality, and performance standards. Second, mandatory quality assurance procedures required the Air Force to inspect and test Fairchild's work item-by-item; if any deliverable failed technical testing, the Air Force possessed the express contractual right to reject the work, compel Fairchild to correct the defect at its own expense, or accept the item at a reduced price. Third, Fairchild was entitled to payment only for work delivered to and accepted by the Air Force; unless and until it "fully succeeded in each phase of the project" it had no right to payment, and it had no right to retain progress payments made during performance if the contract line items to which they applied were not delivered and accepted.

By contrast, neither the Cherry Island Contract nor the WM Contract contained item-by-item technical acceptance testing, express rejection language tied to research failure, or clawback provisions requiring Geosyntec to refund monthly payments if the overall project failed. Geosyntec's assertion that its contracts contained "strong client rejection rights" failed because the right to dispute sums shown on an invoice did not equate to a requirement that its work product be evaluated and accepted prior to payment; under the WM Contract, even an item disputed for suspected defective or negligent work was only temporarily deleted and had to be paid once the dispute was settled, and WM's general right to review and approve work was passive and did not inform Geosyntec's right to payment.
Unconditional Monthly Invoicing Schedules Tied to Inputs Rather Than Outputs

A critical evidentiary failure in Geosyntec was the structural mechanics of the invoicing provisions. Under the WM Contract, Geosyntec submitted monthly progress invoices for all work performed during the previous calendar month, and under the Cherry Island Contract it submitted monthly "approvable" invoices for services rendered, with the pay rate for each item of work pre-determined by the project budget. These invoices were payable upon submission unless an item or sum shown due on the invoice was in dispute. The Eleventh Circuit observed that Geosyntec was paid upon submission of an approvable invoice or for all work performed in the previous month, not upon delivery and acceptance of results meeting contract specifications, so payment for labor inputs rather than accepted technical outputs was not linked to research success. Any risk of nonpayment faced by Geosyntec, such as DSWA declining to pay for work outside the approved scope performed without written permission, was "unrelated to the outcome of its research".
Strict Four-Corners Contractual Interpretation and Downstream Four-Part Test Implications

Because the parties stipulated that the contracts governed the funding issue, the Eleventh Circuit strictly applied the plain-meaning rule of contract interpretation, reiterating that where contractual language is plain, a court should not create confusion by adding hidden meanings, terms, conditions, or unexpressed intentions. Consequently, the court declined to read a success contingency into contracts that did not expressly mandate a successful outcome; as Geosyntec acknowledged at oral argument, the success or failure of its appeal lay in the terms of the two capped contracts, and even contractual obligations to correct omissions or reperform erroneous work at Geosyntec's own expense did not make payment contingent on success.

Furthermore, while the procedural posture of Geosyntec halted at the threshold "funded research" exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) without reaching the substantive four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), the Eleventh Circuit's critique of Geosyntec's contracts exposes a critical third-order vulnerability for engineering and consulting firms. When a contract leaves design "almost entirely to Geosyntec's professional expertise... subject to general (and, at times, passive) requirements" and bills by routine task codes, the taxpayer simultaneously undermines its evidentiary foundation for the substantive four-part test. Although the Eleventh Circuit itself acknowledged that each Cherry Island task required research, development, and testing and did not rule on whether the activities qualified, passive client requirements and routine professional standard-of-care clauses can invite an examiner to argue under the I.R.C. § 174 uncertainty test that the capability, method, or appropriate design was already achievable through standard engineering practice rather than fraught with objective technological uncertainty. Similarly, task-based monthly billing records that fail to segregate iterative hypothesis testing from routine site assessment, data tabulation, and report drafting prevent the taxpayer from proving under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) that "substantially all" (80% or more) of the research activities constituted a scientific-method process of experimentation. Finally, holistic project caps without component-level technical specifications prevent a taxpayer from invoking the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) if the overall project (such as an entire landfill expansion) fails to qualify as a single business component, leaving the taxpayer unable to isolate QREs to discrete, qualifying sub-components.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement examined in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States (and its immediate regulatory ecosystem under I.R.C. § 41) against the taxpayer's specific contractual or evidentiary failure and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Eleventh Circuit.

The Court's Governing Standard of Proof

cells: Funded Research Exclusion (General Rule)
Sought a $1,677,432 federal income tax refund under § 41 for client projects without demonstrating that payment under the capped contracts was contingent on the success of its research.

The taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving that research performed under a third-party contract is not "funded". As with all tax credits, the claimant bears the burden of establishing entitlement; the inquiry turns on the contract terms between researcher and client.
Financial Risk of Research Failure vs. Cost-of-Performance Risk
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Fairchild Indus., Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995)
Argued that maximum price ceilings ($9,991,578 on Cherry Island; $18,781 on WM) exposed Geosyntec to the financial risk of budget cost overruns or failing to earn the full ceiling price.

Cost-of-performance (budget overrun) risk and loss of profit opportunity are legally irrelevant. The taxpayer must prove that its right to payment is contingent on the technical success of the research, such that it bears the financial loss if the research fails to yield the desired result.
"Successful Performance" vs. "Proper Performance"
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)
Relied on contractual provisions requiring "proper performance of each task," adherence to a general professional standard of care, and compliance with applicable codes and regulations.

A general professional standard of care and assurances that work will be free from negligence, error, or defects "do not mandate success," and neither contract equated "proper performance" with "successful performance". The Cherry Island Contract provided no barometer by which performance could be considered "successful" and no mechanism for acceptance or rejection of the delivered design.
Technical Specifications & Item-by-Item Quality Assurance
Fairchild Indus., 71 F.3d at 870–71; Geosyntec, 776 F.3d at 1340–41
Cherry Island design was left to Geosyntec's professional expertise under passive requirements; WM Contract paid for bench testing and a feasibility report even if EISB proved technically unfeasible.

The court contrasted Fairchild, where over 1,000 pages of specifications applied and all work was subject to item-by-item inspection and testing prior to acceptance, with payment made only after acceptance.
Client Rejection Rights & Deliverables Acceptance
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Geosyntec, 776 F.3d at 1341–43

Pointed to invoice dispute provisions allowing DSWA to withhold disputed sums and WM to dispute items for any reason, including suspected defective or negligently performed work (with disputed items only temporarily deleted).

The right to dispute sums shown due on an invoice does not equate to a requirement that work product be evaluated and accepted prior to payment. In Fairchild, by contrast, the client could reject unacceptable work, require correction at the researcher's expense, or accept it at a reduced price, and paid only after acceptance.
Payment Structure & Refundability of Progress Advances
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Geosyntec, 776 F.3d at 1342–43

Billed monthly (approvable invoices for services rendered on Cherry Island; progress invoices for all work performed in the prior month at fixed unit prices on WM), payable upon submission unless disputed, without clawback or refund conditions.

Periodic invoice-based payment schedules for pre-defined tasks at pre-defined rates indicate funded research. The court noted that in Fairchild the contractor had no right to retain progress payments if the line items to which they applied were not delivered and accepted.
Contractual Four-Corners Rule & Parol Evidence
Federal Common Law / State Contract Interpretation Principles (Geosyntec, 776 F.3d at 1341)
Attempted to infer implied performance contingencies and strong rejection rights not explicitly stated in the plain text of the capped agreements.

Courts determine funding status strictly from the plain meaning of the written agreement. Where the language is plain, a court should not create confusion by adding hidden meanings, terms, conditions, or unexpressed intentions to manufacture a payment contingency.
Retention of Substantial Rights in Research
I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3); Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)

Not adjudicated: by stipulation the parties deferred the substantial rights issue because Geosyntec's retained rights varied among its contracts and the issue did not lend itself to summary judgment, and agreed that judgment would enter for the United States if the research was funded regardless of retained rights.

In addition to bearing financial risk, the contract must preserve the taxpayer's "substantial rights" in the research—meaning the legal right to use or exploit the research results in future business without paying a royalty or fee to the client.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the Eleventh Circuit's holding in Geosyntec into actionable legal and technical compliance, the following two applied case studies examine realistic engineering and environmental remediation projects that initially suffer from the exact contractual and evidentiary flaws that disqualified the Cherry Island Contract and the WM Contract. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial blueprint covering project governance, contract redrafting, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking to satisfy both the unfunded research mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) and the substantive four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1).
Case Study 1: Geotechnical & Environmental Infrastructure Engineering (Remedying the "Cherry Island Contract" Pitfalls)
Project Scenario and Initial Disqualifying Structure

TerraCore GeoEngineering, Inc. ("TerraCore"), a U.S. civil and environmental engineering firm, is engaged by a regional municipal solid waste authority ("Authority") to engineer a vertical and lateral expansion of a municipal landfill situated over highly compressible, saturated estuarine clay and submerged lower-layer municipal solid waste, comparable to the soft foundation that limited vertical expansion at the Cherry Island Landfill. The expansion requires designing an integrated sub-base stabilization matrix using prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs), a multi-layer geosynthetic clay liner (GCL), and a high-overburden leachate collection network capable of withstanding saturated waste unit weights of to at depths exceeding 15 meters.

In its initial unrevised state, TerraCore's engagement exhibits four disqualifying features modeled on the Cherry Island Contract in Geosyntec. First, the contract is structured as a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee agreement with a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) cap of $8.5 million, broken into phase sub-caps. Second, TerraCore submits monthly invoices for actual engineering labor hours and direct expenses incurred during the prior month, payable within 30 days unless the Authority disputes an accounting error. Third, the contract's performance covenant merely states that TerraCore shall perform its engineering services consistent with the professional skill and care ordinarily provided by geotechnical engineers practicing in the same locality under similar circumstances and in compliance with state environmental permitting regulations. Fourth, engineers log all hours to a single holistic project billing code ("Project 402 - Landfill Expansion Design") with generic narrative descriptions such as "Soil stability calculations and CAD drafting". Under Geosyntec, the IRS would disallow 100% of TerraCore's claimed QREs on summary judgment: the $8.5 million cap merely creates cost-of-performance risk, monthly billing guarantees payment for effort rather than results, and the standard-of-care clause requires only "proper performance" rather than "successful performance".
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Contractual Pricing and Payment Contingency Restructuring

To overcome the funded research exclusion, TerraCore must eliminate the cost-plus monthly reimbursement structure and replace it with a Milestone-Gated, Contingent Fixed-Price Engineering Deliverable Agreement that explicitly shifts the financial risk of research failure onto TerraCore. All provisions entitling TerraCore to payment based on monthly labor hours incurred or unit tasks performed must be excised, tying compensation exclusively to the delivery, rigorous testing, and formal written acceptance of discrete Engineering Design Deliverables. Because an engineering firm requires working capital during a multi-year infrastructure project, the contract may provide for interim progress advances, but must legally structure them as conditional, unliquidated advances patterned directly on Fairchild Industries. Specifically, the redrafted payment clause must stipulate that all interim milestone payments made by the Authority to TerraCore prior to Final System Acceptance constitute conditional financing advances, and that TerraCore's right to retain any interim advance is strictly contingent upon the technical success of TerraCore's research and design as verified under the contract's Technical Acceptance & Performance Barometers. The clause must further mandate that if any Deliverable fails to achieve the mandatory technical specifications in Appendix B and TerraCore is unable to cure such technical failure at its sole expense within 60 days, the Authority shall reject the Deliverable, terminate the relevant scope, and compel TerraCore to refund all conditional advances previously paid for that Business Component within 30 days of rejection.
Step 2: Replacing "Proper Performance" with Objective Technical Barometers ("Successful Performance")

To overcome the Eleventh Circuit's critique that passive design requirements and general standards of care do not mandate success, TerraCore must segregate its general professional liability covenant from a binding Technical Specification & Acceptance Protocol (Appendix B) modeled on Fairchild. Appendix B must stipulate that the Authority has no obligation to accept or pay for the design unless third-party geotechnical peer review and field pilot-cell instrumentation verify that the engineered design achieves rigorous, quantitative barometers of success across each discrete sub-component. Furthermore, the contract must incorporate an express inspection and rejection clause providing that Deliverables are never deemed accepted upon submission; rather, following delivery of each Design Package and completion of field test-pad instrumentation, the Authority's Independent Technical Review Board must inspect and test the design against the quantitative barometers in Appendix B. If the design fails any technical barometer, the Authority issues a Notice of Technical Rejection and may either require TerraCore to re-engineer and re-test the rejected component entirely at TerraCore's uncompensated expense, or reject the work permanently without payment and demand full restitution of prior advances.

body.text: Step 3: Securing "Substantial Rights" Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)

Because public authorities typically demand ownership of physical construction blueprints, TerraCore must carefully draft the Intellectual Property clause so that it retains "substantial rights" in the underlying research under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000). The contract should grant the Authority title to the site-specific physical permit drawings and a perpetual license to construct and operate the landfill facility, while explicitly reserving to TerraCore sole ownership and perpetual, unrestricted, royalty-free commercial rights to all underlying geotechnical research, finite-element constitutive models, PVD spacing algorithms, shear-strength data correlations, and engineering techniques developed during the engagement, with the unrestricted right to utilize and exploit such research results on engagements for other clients without notice or compensation to the Authority.
Step 4: Project Governance, Business Component Segregation, and Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) and protect against judicial skepticism under the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), TerraCore must restructure its internal project governance prior to commencing work. Rather than billing to a single project code, TerraCore establishes a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) segregated into the three standalone Business Components identified in Appendix B (BC-402.1, BC-402.2, and BC-402.3) under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), while isolating non-qualifying routine activities—such as topographical surveying, environmental permit application formatting, vendor bid administration, and construction observation—into a non-R&D code (BC-402.0 - Routine Project Administration).

At project inception, the Principal Geotechnical Engineer executes a formal, contemporaneous Section 174 Technical Uncertainty Charter for each Business Component documenting why standard engineering codes and existing soil mechanics equations cannot resolve the design challenge—specifically noting that standard one-dimensional Terzaghi consolidation models fail to predict non-linear secondary compression of submerged, heterogeneous municipal waste interacting with marine clay under loads. Throughout design execution, engineers maintain a contemporaneous Experimentation Matrix for each Business Component recording the specific engineering hypothesis formulated (for example, that triangular PVD spacing at intervals coupled with a biaxial geogrid bridging layer will limit differential settlement to ), the computer simulation (PLAXIS 3D finite-element modeling) or laboratory direct-shear test executed, the quantitative test result (such as Iteration 1 failing at differential settlement and inducing tensile rupture in the GCL), and the subsequent design modification. Finally, engineers record hours daily via bi-weekly timecard attestations tied to the specific sub-component and experimental iteration, ensuring that 80% or more ("substantially all") of the hours captured in each Business Component directly reflect a scientific-method process of experimentation.
Case Study 2: Industrial Chemical & Bioremediation Process Development (Remedying the "WM Contract" Pitfalls)
Project Scenario and Initial Disqualifying Structure

BioCleanse Remediation Technologies, LLC ("BioCleanse"), an environmental biotechnology and chemical engineering firm, is engaged by a national industrial manufacturing corporation ("IndustrialCorp") to evaluate and develop an enhanced in situ biogeochemical remediation (EISB) process to degrade a dense non-aqueous phase liquid (DNAPL) plume composed of recalcitrant trichloroethylene (TCE) and co-mingled 1,4-dioxane in fractured bedrock aquifers beneath an active manufacturing plant, mirroring the WM Contract for groundwater cleanup in Niagara, New York.

In its initial unrevised state, BioCleanse's contract replicates the exact legal defects of the WM Contract in Geosyntec. First, the scope of work requires BioCleanse to perform laboratory microcosm bench tests evaluating whether a novel combination of organohalide-respiring bacteria (Dehalococcoides strains) and zero-valent iron (ZVI) nanoparticles can degrade the site contaminants, and to submit a final report tabulating the data, interpreting methodology, and discussing potential pilot-test designs. Second, total compensation is capped at $185,000, and BioCleanse submits monthly invoices reimbursed "upon proper performance of each laboratory task at the fixed unit prices set forth in the Estimated Budget". Third, nothing in the agreement requires the bioremediation technology to actually succeed in order for BioCleanse to be paid; if the laboratory bench tests demonstrate that the high salinity and low pH of the bedrock groundwater completely inhibit microbial dechlorination, BioCleanse still collects the full $185,000 upon delivering the report explaining why the technology proved unfeasible. Under Geosyntec, this contract is per se funded research because IndustrialCorp is paying for the performance of research tasks rather than a successful product or result, placing 100% of the financial risk of failed research on the client.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Transforming a "Feasibility Study Service" into a "Contingent Process & Formulation Delivery Contract"

BioCleanse cannot claim the R&D credit if the contractual deliverable is merely an evaluative report summarizing laboratory test data. BioCleanse must restructure the commercial transaction from a research service agreement into a Contingent Custom Process & Chemical Formulation Sale Agreement under Treas. Reg. §§ 1.41-4A(d)(1) and 1.41-2(e)(2). The redrafted agreement must specify that IndustrialCorp is purchasing a Validated, Site-Specific Biogeochemical Remediation Process and Custom Amendment Formulation (the "Deliverable Process"), rather than laboratory testing services or a feasibility study. Crucially, the contract must explicitly reverse the risk allocation that doomed the WM Contract in Geosyntec by stipulating that payment of the $185,000 Contract Price is strictly contingent upon BioCleanse delivering a validated EISB/ZVI formulation and injection protocol that achieves the Mandatory Contaminant Destruction Thresholds set forth in Schedule 1. If BioCleanse's laboratory bench testing and column simulations demonstrate that the proposed biogeochemical process cannot achieve the Schedule 1 thresholds under site groundwater conditions, BioCleanse bears the entire financial loss of its research expenditures, no fee is owed by IndustrialCorp, and BioCleanse must immediately refund any conditional milestone deposits.
Step 2: Eliminating Unit-Price Task Invoicing and Establishing Hard Chemical Acceptance Criteria

BioCleanse must eliminate the "fixed unit price per task" budget schedule that the Eleventh Circuit cited as proof of funded research. In addition, because the Geosyntec court noted that WM could change the work by written directive, with any necessary price increase agreed by addendum, so the ceiling price was not immovable—the redrafted BioCleanse contract must strictly prohibit upward price adjustments for additional laboratory iterations: if the initial five microcosm formulations fail to meet Schedule 1, BioCleanse is legally obligated to fund and execute subsequent iterations at its own uncompensated expense to earn the contract price. Furthermore, the requirement for "proper performance of each task" must be replaced with objective chemical engineering acceptance metrics in Schedule 1, verified by an independent EPA-certified analytical laboratory prior to client acceptance and payment.

body.text: Step 3: Structuring Intellectual Property to Preserve Substantial Rights

To satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), the agreement must ensure that BioCleanse does not transfer exclusive ownership of the resulting chemical formulation or microbial process to IndustrialCorp. The contract grants IndustrialCorp a non-exclusive, site-specific license to inject and deploy the validated Deliverable Process at its manufacturing facility, while BioCleanse explicitly retains all patents, trade secrets, microbial strain improvements, surfactant-stabilized ZVI synthesis techniques, and empirical reaction kinetics data, with the unrestricted right to commercialize the formulation for other industrial clients without paying royalties or seeking consent from IndustrialCorp.
Step 4: Laboratory Governance and Scientific Method Substantiation

To ensure the underlying laboratory costs—comprising W-2 scientist wages under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and consumable laboratory chemicals and supplies under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)—survive a substantive IRS audit under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) and I.R.C. § 174, BioCleanse must implement rigorous laboratory governance. Initial site groundwater sampling and baseline chemical characterization (determining existing pH, oxidation-reduction potential, and contaminant concentrations) are segregated into a separate, non-claimed administrative phase. QRE tracking commences only after baseline data establishes objective technological uncertainty—specifically, that existing commercial emulsified vegetable oil (EVO) and standard Dehalococcoides bioaugmentation cultures undergo complete metabolic arrest due to the site's extreme sulfate concentrations () and co-mingled 1,4-dioxane toxicity.

Each microcosm and column reactor trial is assigned a unique Experimental Protocol ID tied directly to the general ledger and payroll system. In Protocol BIO-101, scientists formulate and document the hypothesis that coating micro-scale ZVI with a biodegradable carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) polymer at a weight ratio will buffer sulfide toxicity and sustain Dehalococcoides reductive dehalogenase enzyme activity in high-sulfate groundwater, recording exact reagent masses, control versus variable reactor setups, daily redox and pH telemetry, and GC-MS analytical runs. When Protocol BIO-101 fails at day 18 because sulfate-reducing bacteria outcompete dechlorinators for hydrogen donors and stall degradation at cis-DCE, the laboratory notebook logs the analytical failure and documents the scientific rationale for formulating Protocol BIO-102, which incorporates molybdate as a specific metabolic inhibitor of sulfate reduction combined with a slow-release lactide hydrogen donor. All consumable laboratory supplies (chemical reagents, isotopic tracers, bedrock core columns, and GC-MS calibration standards) are requisitioned via purchase orders stamped with the specific Experimental Protocol ID, and laboratory microbiologists and chemical engineers allocate their daily time entries across the specific Protocol IDs rather than generic "WM Bench Testing" task codes, establishing an unbroken evidentiary chain linking the contractual risk of failure to a rigorous process of experimentation.
Comparative Summary of Remedial Transformations

The following table synthesizes the structural transformations executed across both case studies to convert disqualifying "funded" contracts under Geosyntec into fully compliant, audit-ready R&D tax credit claims.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The Eleventh Circuit's ruling in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States—and its subsequent adoption by the Fifth Circuit in Grigsby, the Eighth Circuit in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and the United States Tax Court—cements a strict, text-driven doctrine for R&D tax credit claims involving third-party contracts. Tax advisors and corporate counsel can no longer rely on the economic reality that capped contracts (and, under later decisions such as Grigsby and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, fixed-price contracts) expose a firm to financial losses when projects require unexpected engineering rework, although the Geosyntec district court found the fixed-price contracts before it unfunded and that ruling was not appealed. Under federal tax law, budget overrun exposure is mere cost-of-performance risk.

To survive IRS examination and summary judgment in federal court, taxpayers performing custom engineering, software development, architectural design, or scientific contract research must align their commercial agreements with the explicit mandates of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) before research activities commence. By embedding quantitative technical barometers of success, formal item-by-item inspection and rejection clauses, refundable progress advance mechanisms, and explicit reservations of substantial IP rights directly into the four corners of their client contracts—and pairing those terms with component-level scientific experimentation logs—taxpayers can decisively establish that they bear the financial risk of research failure and secure their entitlement to the I.R.C. § 41 research credit.
